rewritten_text:
Biddy cried. My own eyes blurred the darkening garden, the lane, and the stars beginning to appear.

‘Nothing was ever found out, Biddy?’

‘Nothing.’

‘Do you know what has happened to Orlick?’

‘Judging by the colour of his clothes, I think he must be working in the quarries.’

‘Then you’ve seen him, of course? Why are you looking at that dark tree in the lane?’

‘I saw him there the night she died.’

‘And that wasn’t the last time, Biddy?’

‘No. I saw him there while we were walking here. There’s no point,’ she added, putting her hand on my arm as I started to rush out. ‘You know I wouldn’t mislead you. He stayed less than a minute, and now he’s gone.’

Finding that this man still followed her filled me with fresh anger, and I felt a deep hatred for him. I told her so, saying that I would spend any amount of money and go to any trouble to drive him out of the district. Little by little she guided our conversation towards calmer subjects. She told me how much Joe loved me and how he never complained about anything. She did not say ‘about me’; she had no need, for I understood. He simply did his duty in his daily life, with strong hands, few words, and a gentle heart.

‘You really can’t praise him too much,’ I said. ‘And Biddy, we must talk about these things often. Naturally I’ll be coming here frequently now. I won’t leave poor Joe alone.’

Biddy did not say a word.

‘Biddy, did you hear me?’

‘Yes, Mr. Pip.’

‘Quite apart from calling me Mr. Pip—which I think is in poor taste, Biddy—what do you mean?’

‘What do I mean?’ Biddy asked timidly.

‘Biddy,’ I said, firmly convinced of my own good intentions, ‘I must ask you to explain what you mean by this.’

‘By this?’ she said.

‘Please don’t repeat everything,’ I replied sharply. ‘You never used to do that, Biddy.’

‘Used to!’ said Biddy. ‘Oh, Mr. Pip! Used to!’

Well, I thought it best to drop that argument too. After another silent walk around the garden, I returned to my main point.

‘Biddy, when I said I’d be coming here often to see Joe, you were noticeably silent. Please tell me why.’

‘Are you quite certain you really will come often?’ Biddy asked, stopping on the narrow garden path and looking at me beneath the stars with clear, honest eyes.

Yet he kept one secret from these dear friends, a secret he had cherished since his earliest years. Although he loved his fellow students, he did not trust any of them to treat it with enough sensitivity or understanding. He was in love. He feared they might laugh at the strength of his feelings. He could not bear to have them dishonour his love by treating it as something slight and temporary, when to him it was the very centre of his life.

Near his family’s mansion lived a gentleman of modest means who had three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, but her beauty was only one of her gifts. She had a clear, strong mind and an almost angelically gentle nature. She and my father had played together since infancy. Even as a child, Diana had been a favourite of his mother’s. His mother grew still fonder of this beautiful, lively girl as she grew older, so the two were always together during his school and college holidays. Novels and the other ways that young people in civilised society learn about passion before experiencing it had deeply affected him, for he was unusually open to every influence. At eleven, Diana was his favourite playmate, but he already spoke to her in the language of love. She was almost two years older, yet her upbringing had left her more childlike, at least in understanding and expressing feelings. She innocently accepted his passionate declarations and returned them without knowing what they meant. She had read no novels and spent time only with her younger sisters. How could she know the difference between friendship and love? By the time her growing understanding revealed the true nature of their relationship, she already loved him. Her only fear was that some new attraction, or a change in his feelings, would make him break the promises he had made as a child.

Instead, those promises grew warmer and more tender every day. His love had grown as he grew, becoming woven into every ability and feeling, so that only death could end it. No one knew of it but the two of them. He dreaded his companions’ criticism in everything, including their disapproval of his deep love for someone less wealthy than himself. Even so, nothing ever weakened, for a single moment, his determination to marry her. He meant to do so as soon as he could gather the courage to face the difficulties he was resolved to overcome.

Diana fully deserved the deepest love he could give her.

He could not stop himself. And it drove him furious to think that Becky Thatcher seemed completely unaware he even existed. But she did notice him. She knew she was winning their battle, and she was pleased to see him suffering as she had suffered.

Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom hinted that he had things to do, things that could not wait, and time was running out. It was useless; she went on talking. ‘Oh, hang her,’ Tom thought. ‘Am I ever going to get away?’ Finally he said he really must attend to his business. She innocently replied that she would be ‘around’ when school ended, and he hurried off, hating her for saying it.

‘Any other boy!’ he thought, grinding his teeth. ‘Anybody in town except that show-off from Saint Louis, who thinks his fancy clothes make him a nobleman! All right, mister. I beat you up the first day you came here, and I’ll do it again! Just wait till I catch you outside! I’ll take you and—’

He began beating an imaginary boy, punching the air, kicking, and digging with his fingers. ‘Oh, you do, do you? You’ve had enough, have you? Well, let that teach you!’ At last he finished the imaginary beating, satisfied.

At noon Tom escaped home. His conscience could stand no more of Amy’s grateful happiness, and his jealousy could bear no more of the other misery. Becky went back to looking at pictures with Alfred. But as the minutes dragged by without Tom appearing to suffer, her pleasure in winning began to fade. She lost interest, became serious and distracted, and then grew sad. Two or three times a footstep made her listen eagerly, but each hope proved false. Tom never came. Finally she felt thoroughly miserable and wished she had not gone so far. Poor Alfred could see that he was losing her attention, though he did not understand why. He kept crying, ‘Here’s a good one! Look at this!’ At last her patience snapped. ‘Oh, stop bothering me! I don’t care about them!’ she said, bursting into tears and getting up to walk away.

Alfred came alongside her, intending to comfort her, but she said:

‘Can’t you go away and leave me alone? I hate you!’

He stopped, wondering what he had done. She had promised to look at pictures throughout the lunch break. She went on walking and crying, while Alfred wandered thoughtfully into the empty schoolhouse. He felt humiliated and angry. It was easy to guess the truth: she had simply used him to take revenge on Tom Sawyer.
